questions.q: In the OpportunityCloseService lab scenario, why does the test class need a registered HttpCalloutMock even for the positive 'closes valid Opportunity' test?
options: Mocks are only needed for negative tests
The method under test makes an outbound HTTP callout, and test methods cannot make real callouts without a mock registered
HttpCalloutMock is required by Apex for every test class regardless of what the code does
It isn't actually needed in this scenario
questions.explain: OpportunityCloseService.closeAsWon makes a real outbound callout to notify an external system — any test exercising this method, positive or negative, needs a mock registered or it will throw a CalloutException.

questions.q: Why does the zero-Amount test wrap the call to closeAsWon in a try/catch expecting a DmlException, rather than just calling the method directly?
options: Because addError() on a record surfaces as a DmlException when the subsequent DML statement runs, and the test needs to prove that rejection actually happens
Because DmlException is thrown automatically by every Apex method
Because try/catch is required syntax for all @isTest methods
Because the mock callout throws this exception
questions.explain: addError() marks the record with an error that surfaces as a DmlException once the update statement executes — the negative test proves this rejection path, following the Lesson 12 pattern.

questions.q: What does the bulk test (processesTwoHundredOpportunitiesInOneTransaction) specifically prove that the single-record positive test does not?
options: That the HTTP callout returns a 200 status
That the service correctly processes a realistic batch size in a single transaction, not just one record at a time
That the Opportunity's StageName field exists
That addError() works correctly
questions.explain: The bulk test specifically proves the method handles 200 records correctly in one transaction — a scenario the single-record positive test can't reveal, per Lesson 8's bulk-safety concerns.

questions.q: According to the lesson's self-review checklist, which of the following should a finished test class NOT contain?
options: A negative test for every business rule
A bulk test at a realistic record count
Any hardcoded record Ids
Mocked callouts instead of real ones
questions.explain: The self-review checklist explicitly calls for zero hardcoded Ids anywhere in a finished test class, consistent with Lesson 14's warning about hardcoded Id fragility.

questions.q: In the @TestSetup method used in this lab, when does the 'Zero Deal' Opportunity's data actually get rolled back?
options: Immediately after each test method that touches it finishes, or at the end of the whole test class if unmodified — consistent with @TestSetup's documented rollback behavior
It is never rolled back and persists after the test class finishes
It is rolled back the moment the test class starts, before any test method runs
@TestSetup data is rolled back only if SeeAllData=true is also specified
questions.explain: Per Lesson 6, @TestSetup data is shared across test methods, with any per-method changes rolled back after that method, and the baseline rolled back once at the end of the whole class's execution.
